newsitem.title: GEORGIA: Georgia urges Russia to return ex-security chief.
newsitem.headline: Georgia urges Russia to return ex-security chief.

text.p: Georgia on Friday demanded that Russia hand over a former security minister it says planned an assassination attempt on President Eduard Shevardnadze, as well as cash for arms it says were stolen by Moscow.
Georgia has been pressing Russia to produce Igor Giorgadze since he disappeared days after the August, 1995, bomb attack on Shevardnadze's motorcade which left the leader with cuts and bruises.
But Friday's letter brought a usually low-key effort to a higher pitch.

Georgia insists Giorgadze is hiding in Moscow with the help of Russian security officials. The Russian authorities say they cannot find him, though Giorgadze has given numerous interviews to the Russian media since the attack.

"We have repeatedly contacted you by telephone, had meetings with you and even given you the exact location of Igor Giorgadze in Moscow...but you say you cannot find him," said a four-page letter sent by the Georgian chief prosecutor, Dzhamlet Babilashvili, to his Russian counterpart, Yuri Skuratov.
A copy of the letter was obtained by Reuters in Tbilisi on Friday.
Officials in the Russian prosecutor's office in Moscow could not be immediately reached for comment.

"From Moscow Giorgadze is continuing to engage in anti-Georgian activities and calling for the overthrow of the government. The passivity of the Russian law enforcement bodies is in violation of international conventions," it said.
Georgian authorities say late last year they detained a group of 11 "terrorists" under Giorgadze's command that had planned bomb attacks on the Tbilisi subway system and other violent acts.

Georgia says Giorgadze, a 25-year veteran of the Soviet KGB and the son of the leader of Georgia's small Communist Party, plotted with hardliners in Moscow who hate Shevardnadze for his role in hastening the breakup of the Soviet Union when he was Mikhail Gorbachev's foreign minister.
It says Giorgadze was spirited away by airplane to Russia by military officials still based in the former Soviet republic.
Russia has always denied the charges.

Also on Friday, the head of Georgia's parliamentary security commission called on Russia to return what he alleged was $4 billion worth of weapons its military took from Georgia after the demise of the Soviet Union.

Revaz Adamia told journalists Russia had taken away fighter aircraft, naval vessels, and other military equipment. He said the commission had discussed the transfers during a closed session on Thursday evening and that cash compensation should be given if the arms are not returned.
Relations between Moscow and Tbilisi have never been smooth since Georgia got independence after the breakup of the Communist empire in 1991.

They seem to have set off on a new downward spiral by Georgian demands that 1,500 Russian peacekeepers start leaving its breakaway province of Abkhazia after July 31 unless they agree to take on wider functions such as helping refugees resettle to the region and patrolling a bigger zone.
So far Russia has declined the new role in Abkhazia, a de facto independent state since 1993 after a year-long war with Georgian forces that killed more than 10,000 people.
